cards.title: Give the platform enough shows before judging it
cards.summary: Consistency across many shows is required to generate enough platform data and followers; two shows is not a verdict.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to continue or quit a live-selling channel after early weak results.

cards.title: Use platform first-seller incentives as launch runway
cards.summary: Whatnot's fast approval and first-show sales matching reduce the cost of testing live selling with no audience.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to start selling on Whatnot and planning the economics of your first show.

cards.title: Handle shipping labels and weight verification in-app
cards.summary: After a live sale, verify item weight, generate the label, and fix label paper size in settings before printing.
cards.use_when: Fulfilling an item sold in a live-selling stream on Whatnot.

cards.title: Handle the negative-margin mindset: accept lower prices while audience grows
cards.summary: Early live-selling prices may sit well below static-marketplace value; the source frames that gap as a deliberate trade for audience and repeat buyers.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations for pricing and margin during the first weeks of a live-selling channel.

cards.title: Pick one category-appropriate item and a simple thumbnail for the test show
cards.summary: For a cold-start test, list in the most relevant category with one honest photo and a curiosity title rather than optimizing for search.
cards.use_when: Setting up the listing, category and title for a single-item live show with no follower base.

cards.title: Hook's real job: filter for the right buyer, not just stop the scroll
cards.summary: Design hooks to attract the correct target audience so Meta optimizes toward real buyers rather than generic viewers.
cards.use_when: Planning the opening 3 seconds of a paid social video ad or writing hook variations for a Meta campaign and deciding who the hook should call out.

cards.title: Three elements of a hook: audio, copy, visual
cards.summary: Treat each hook as three adjustable components and change one at a time to lift hook rate.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a paid social ad's hook underperforms, or generating hook variants for a video or static ad without re-shooting everything.

cards.title: Plug-and-play hook template: Persona + Problem + Pattern Interrupt + Promise
cards.summary: A four-part hook structure that filters the audience, agitates the problem, retains attention, and gives a reason to keep watching.
cards.use_when: Writing a first draft hook for an ecommerce ad from scratch, or briefing an LLM or creator to generate hook copy at volume.

cards.title: Common hook types and when to use each
cards.summary: A working set of hook categories — contrarian truth, specific proof, common mistakes, high-stakes warning, curiosity gap, tactical promise, mythbusting objection — with notes on ecommerce fit.
cards.use_when: Choosing an angle for a new ecommerce ad, or generating a set of hook variations to test against a control.

cards.title: Grade hooks on clarity, relevance, novelty — then specificity, credibility
cards.summary: A five-criteria scoring rubric in order of importance for judging whether a hook is worth running.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a batch of ecommerce ad hooks before production, or deciding which of several hook concepts to put spend behind.

cards.title: Diagnosing a failing hook: the case of the audio-only jerky hook
cards.summary: A worked example showing how a scroll-stopping curiosity gap can fail because it doesn't attract the right audience or convey clarity and relevance.
cards.use_when: Auditing a live ecommerce ad hook that is getting views but not converting, and deciding whether to rewrite the angle entirely.

cards.title: Specificity in the hook: 'two problems' beats 'some problems'
cards.summary: Concrete numbers and constraints in the hook increase trust and hold viewers longer than generic phrasing.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing ecommerce hook copy where a claim could be made more specific — e.g., number of problems, reasons, steps or results.

cards.title: Turning one hook script into dozens of variations via visual and copy swaps
cards.summary: Vary visual and overlay copy independently to multiply hook variants and discover which combination performs.
cards.use_when: Running creative testing on an ecommerce video ad when the audio script is working but hook rate is flat, or when you need volume of hook variations cheaply.

cards.title: The product awareness curve: keep awareness near zero through the hook and let it rise slowly
cards.summary: Map how aware the viewer is that they're being sold to, and keep it low through the hook, gently rising toward the CTA.
cards.use_when: Structuring the full script of an ecommerce video ad — particularly deciding when the product should first appear on screen.

cards.title: Bridging the hook into the body: do not spike into a pitch
cards.summary: The transition from hook to body is where good ads often lose viewers; educate smoothly and embed the product gradually.
cards.use_when: Editing or writing the first 5–15 seconds after the hook of a video ad, and diagnosing retention curve drop-offs.

cards.title: Rewriting a generic product-first hook into a persona-led educational hook
cards.summary: Take a weak product-led hook and rebuild it around the buyer's pain, common failed attempts, and an educational payoff.
cards.use_when: Reworking an ecommerce ad whose hook shows the product immediately and leads with brand claims rather than a customer problem.

cards.title: Frameworks as a starting point, not an end state
cards.summary: Use templates to get your first hooks written, then move off them to find white space competitors can't copy.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to lean on hook templates or invest in original hook development for an ecommerce brand's ad library.

cards.title: Start creative with a customer problem, not a format
cards.summary: Before choosing UGC, static or carousel, mine customer research to find one problem, then let the problem dictate the format.
cards.use_when: Kicking off a new paid-social creative round for a product and you don't yet know which angle or format to produce.

cards.title: Build one ad around one argument, not ten selling points
cards.summary: Packing every selling point into a single ad produces a confusing infomercial; instead pick the single argument for the persona and prove it.
cards.use_when: Writing the script or storyboard for a cold-traffic ad and the draft is accumulating warranty, returns, dimensions, motor speed and every other feature.

cards.title: Match every product claim with visual proof
cards.summary: Any claim made in an ad script needs a corresponding on-screen demonstration, because audiences no longer trust bare assertions.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a finished creative before launch to check whether the claims in the voiceover or copy are actually demonstrated on screen.

cards.title: Write hooks directly from the stated customer problem
cards.summary: Turn the researched customer complaint into the first line of the ad so the right viewer self-selects and keeps listening.
cards.use_when: Drafting hooks and opening seconds for a cold-traffic video ad after you have selected one customer problem.

cards.title: Generate more angles from consistently repeated review themes
cards.summary: Segmenting reviews by use case can multiply a single generic creative into several distinct, proven ad angles.
cards.use_when: A brand has one generic creative and wants more angles without inventing new positioning from scratch.

cards.title: Match creative testing volume to your daily ad spend
cards.summary: Launching dozens of ads on a small budget means most never get distribution, so 'it didn't work' is not a real finding.
cards.use_when: Planning how many new creatives to launch this month given your current daily spend.

cards.title: Don't crown the ad the platform spent the most on
cards.summary: An ad that receives the bulk of spend naturally drives the most sales, so 'winner' must be judged on supporting metrics, not volume.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a creative test where one ad has taken most of the spend and you are about to declare it the winner and scale it.

cards.title: Read CTR and link CTR together to spot empty attention
cards.summary: A high CTR with a large CTR-to-link-CTR drop signals an ad that entertains but fails to explain the product.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether a high-CTR creative is actually driving qualified buying traffic or just capturing attention.

cards.title: Run single-variable creative tests within the same angle
cards.summary: Vary only the delivery format while holding angle and product constant so you can attribute the result to something specific.
cards.use_when: You have a promising angle and want to learn something rather than randomly produce new ads.

cards.title: Diagnose creative through the attention-to-purchase journey
cards.summary: Trace each metric stage — stop, click, post-click behaviour — to locate where the ad or the site is actually failing.
cards.use_when: An ad is underperforming and you need to decide whether to rebuild the creative, the landing page or something else.

cards.title: Use each creative test as the brief for the next round
cards.summary: Every test result should specify what to produce next — more of a winning angle, more of a winning hook, or more of a winning format.
cards.use_when: Scheduling the next creative production round and deciding what the team should actually make.

cards.title: Handpick ads into funnel positions based on supporting metrics
cards.summary: Individual winners serve different funnel roles, and the combination of metrics tells you whether an ad belongs at top, middle or bottom of funnel.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to deploy each winning creative — prospecting versus retargeting — and what budget structure to give it.

cards.title: Four psychological pillars of scroll-stopping Meta ads
cards.summary: Every strong ad must earn attention, open a curiosity gap, trigger an emotion, and signal connection to a specific buyer.
cards.use_when: Drafting or reviewing a new paid social creative for a product launch or existing SKU on Meta.

cards.title: Match ad type to whether the funnel finishes the sale
cards.summary: Problem-heavy, curiosity-driven ads work when a quiz or landing page continues the sell; simple product ads should instead win on attention and shareability.
cards.use_when: Choosing the creative style (dark problem-solving vs. light meme) for a given product and funnel type.

cards.title: Design shareable meme ads that raise AOV
cards.summary: Funny, shareable ad creative lets buyers spread the product and can lift average order value by encouraging friend-to-friend sends.
cards.use_when: Creating acquisition creative for a light-resonance product where you want organic shares or higher basket value.

cards.title: Do days of manual creative research before writing ads
cards.summary: Build a handwritten research document from Reddit, reviews, and comments instead of trusting a five-minute AI research prompt.
cards.use_when: Starting creative production for a new product, niche, or category where you lack buyer language.

cards.title: Write creative briefs with six mandatory fields before producing ads
cards.summary: A structured brief (concept, creative type, angle, headline, CTA, visual direction) prevents making 100 copies of one ad.
cards.use_when: Handing off a static ad to a designer or producing it yourself in Canva.

cards.title: Test ad concepts against a four-question 'made for me' scorecard
cards.summary: A quick checklist confirms an ad speaks to the ICP, opens a curiosity gap, triggers emotion, and shows a path to a solution.
cards.use_when: Pre-launch review of a new creative before you commit spend on Meta.

cards.title: Live Auction Show Planning: Schedule Early, Promote Hard
cards.summary: Schedule live auction shows at least a week ahead and promote across channels to maximize bookmarks, which drives viewer turnout and higher average selling price.
cards.use_when: Planning a live-stream selling event (Whatnot or similar live auction) and deciding how far in advance to schedule and how to promote it.

cards.title: Thumbnail Design: Value Callouts and Brand Recognition
cards.summary: Build the show thumbnail in a free tool like Canva with the biggest incentive and recognizable brand names to win attention while viewers scroll.
cards.use_when: Creating the static thumbnail image for a live auction show listing on a platform where buyers scroll past many shows.

cards.title: Anchor High-Ticket Items Early to Shape Price Perception
cards.summary: Borrow Costco's front-of-store $5,000 TV logic: show your most expensive items first so everything after feels cheap and buyers bid more freely.
cards.use_when: Sequencing items during a live auction show or ordering products on a storefront/landing page to influence perceived value.

cards.title: Use Loss Leaders and Freebies to Pull Buyers Toward Profitable Inventory
cards.summary: Make your money on the 80% of cheap, high-margin items while using giveaway-grade high-value items as the draw.
cards.use_when: Building a product mix for a live sale or promotion where you need traffic and engagement but profit comes from lower-cost goods.

cards.title: Buyer Giveaway Mechanics: Reward Buyers, Incentivize Bids
cards.summary: Gate a giveaway to customers only (a 'buyer's giveaway') so it rewards purchases and nudges non-buyers to bid at least once.
cards.use_when: Designing a giveaway or incentive for a live-stream sale or event to convert viewers into buyers and lift purchase volume.

cards.title: Starting Bids at $1: When It Works and When It Doesn't
cards.summary: $1 starts create excitement only when the room is full; the source says most sellers should not use them.
cards.use_when: Deciding starting bid prices for auction inventory in a live-stream show.

cards.title: Entertainment as Conversion: Costumes, Music, Energy
cards.summary: If viewers have fun they become buyers, and if buyers have fun they become repeat buyers — so build small bits into every show.
cards.use_when: Hosting a live-stream sale and trying to hold viewers, increase engagement, and improve conversion to purchase.

cards.title: Pacing a High-Volume Auction Show
cards.summary: Budget ~45 seconds to 1 minute per item and expect a 250-item show to run close to 4 hours.
cards.use_when: Planning show length, item count, and staffing for a live auction event.

cards.title: Calculate Show Profitability: Gross Sales, Fees, COGS
cards.summary: Track gross sales, platform fees and adjustments, inventory cost, and giveaway cost to get true show profit.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a live-stream sale was actually profitable and planning break-even for the next show.

cards.title: Read Show Health Metrics: Buyers, New Buyers, Concurrents
cards.summary: Use buyers-per-item, first-time buyers, max concurrent viewers, and total unique viewers to judge whether promotion worked.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a completed live sale to diagnose whether your promotion and show design succeeded and what to change next time.

cards.title: Build Inventory Cheap to Protect Auction Margins
cards.summary: Source product from thrift bins, flea markets, and lot deals to keep COGS low enough that even $8–$15 sales are profitable.
cards.use_when: Sourcing inventory for a live auction or resale channel where per-item prices are low and volume is high.

cards.title: Large Show vs. Routine Show: Match Format to Goal
cards.summary: Run small frequent shows for baseline cash and occasional big promoted shows with better inventory to lift ASP and reach new buyers.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a normal weekly live sale or invest in a larger, promoted event.

cards.title: Grow a Following Inside the Platform Without Off-Platform Audiences
cards.summary: A pre-existing social following helps but is not required — sellers can build audience directly on the selling platform.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest time in off-platform promotion or in-platform audience growth for a live-selling channel.

cards.title: Decide if your product needs a VSL ad before producing one
cards.summary: Use the three qualifying conditions—complex product, low-trust category, or new-to-market category—to decide whether a long educational video ad is worth the production cost.
cards.use_when: Choosing an acquisition creative format for a complicated, distrusted, or brand-new product category, versus running standard short ads.

cards.title: The seven-part VSL scripting framework
cards.summary: A repeatable order for scripting a long-form video sales letter: Hook, Problem, Mechanism, Objection Handling, Proof, Risk Reversal, CTA.
cards.use_when: Writing a full VSL ad script for a complex product or low-trust category where doubt must be removed before purchase.

cards.title: Hook is the highest-leverage test in a VSL
cards.summary: Because roughly 80% of viewers drop off before the body script starts, test 3–6 hook variations against a fixed body and CTA rather than rewriting everything.
cards.use_when: Improving performance of an already-produced VSL, or structuring a paid social test plan for a long-form video ad.

cards.title: Mine real customer data for the objection-handling section
cards.summary: Populate the VSL objection section with verbatim customer reasons for almost-not-buying, drawn from reviews, support tickets, post-purchase surveys, and call recordings.
cards.use_when: Writing the objection-handling portion of a VSL script for a product where buyers considered alternatives or hesitated before purchase.

cards.title: Use modular editing to cheaply generate VSL variants
cards.summary: Because VSLs are long, you can move whole sections around and cut multiple durations from one asset to produce more creative tests without new shoots.
cards.use_when: Generating multiple creative variations from a single long-form VSL to test on paid social.

cards.title: Bridge from education to product without a premature pitch
cards.summary: Avoid the common mistake of pivoting straight from the intro to a brand/CTA pitch; earn the right to sell by first building the problem and mechanism.
cards.use_when: Drafting the transition from VSL education into the product introduction so viewers don't disengage early.

cards.title: Avoid the six common VSL scripting mistakes
cards.summary: A checklist of recurring VSL failures: brand-story hook, claims without mechanism, weak proof, vague offer or missing CTA, and slow pacing or unreadable text.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a drafted VSL script or an underperforming VSL before briefing an editor or relaunching.

cards.title: Why some VSLs omit the CTA (and when that's acceptable)
cards.summary: An asset without a CTA is usually an error, but can be deliberate when it feeds an Amazon funnel or a retargeting campaign that handles the close.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to include a CTA on a VSL or whether to run it as top-of-funnel only with a separate retargeting close.

cards.title: Pair each VSL with a matching educational landing page
cards.summary: The VSL narrative must continue onto a contextually relevant advertorial or dedicated landing page—dropping to a generic product page breaks continuity and undercuts the ad.
cards.use_when: Setting up the post-click destination for a VSL campaign or running an advertorial/landing page test.

cards.title: Combine UGC, AI animation, and real footage to build VSL B-roll
cards.summary: VSLs stitch together AI UGC, real UGC, and animated motion graphics to explain complex mechanisms without a dedicated shoot.
cards.use_when: Planning the visual production and B-roll sourcing for a long-form educational VSL ad.

cards.title: Read performance signals: likes, launch age, and frequency
cards.summary: Use public engagement and launch age as rough signals of a VSL's spend level, and frequency as a rough indicator of how cold an ad still is.
cards.use_when: Sourcing winning VSL examples for creative inspiration or assessing whether an ad is still reaching new audiences.

cards.title: Recognize when a VSL script can reorder its sections
cards.summary: The seven-part order is a template, not a fixed sequence—the source's working example moves problem before hook education and mechanism after objection handling.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep or reorder the standard VSL section flow when scripting a new creative.

cards.title: AI Ads: Use Context, Not Volume
cards.summary: Most AI ad generation fails because it produces high-volume generic 'slop' instead of ads built on proven angles and specific customer avatars.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how to deploy AI tools for paid social ad production and are tempted to bulk-generate ads quickly.

cards.title: Avatar + Template = Ad Concept (Creative as Targeting)
cards.summary: Shift from building ads for manual audiences to building ad concepts from an avatar plus a template, letting Meta's algorithm use the creative messaging to find the audience.
cards.use_when: You are structuring new ad concepts and deciding how to organize targeting, ad sets, and messaging intent in your prospecting campaign.

cards.title: Pack-Based Modular Creative Testing Structure
cards.summary: Launch each new round of creatives as a 'pack' ad set grouped by avatar, sized 4–8 ads, inside the prospecting campaign.
cards.use_when: You are setting up prospecting campaign structure and deciding how to organize and isolate new creative rounds.

cards.title: Seven-Day Minimum Budget Constraint to Force Creative Testing
cards.summary: Set an ad-set minimum spend equal to 1x target CPA for 7 days to force the algorithm to test new creatives, then remove it to let winners scale.
cards.use_when: You are launching new creative packs and need to guarantee they get a fair chance at spend rather than being starved by the algorithm.

cards.title: Iteration Engine: Scale Winners from Incremental Revenue Data
cards.summary: Find top ads by incremental revenue and incremental ROAS, then produce meaningful variations—not word-level tweaks—of those winning concepts.
cards.use_when: You have winning ads in the account and want to systematically expand them into new iterations for continued prospecting.

cards.title: What 'Good' AI Ad Output Looks Like
cards.summary: Judge AI ad output by whether it maps to a named, proven angle or format—not by raw volume produced.
cards.use_when: You are reviewing a batch of AI-generated static or video ad concepts and deciding which to run and which to discard.

cards.title: Source winning ad concepts from competitors' longest-running ads
cards.summary: Find proven creative concepts by scanning the Facebook Ad Library or a tool like Magic Brief for competitors' longest-running, highest-spend ads.
cards.use_when: You need new ad concepts to test for your store and are deciding where to source creative inspiration.

cards.title: Recreate competitor concepts as your own catalog variations
cards.summary: Turn a competitor's winning concept into a large batch of on-brand iterations across your own products rather than a single copy.
cards.use_when: You have identified a competitor ad that has run a long time and want to convert it into testable creative for your store's catalog.

cards.title: Launch new ads as isolated 'packs' inside a prospecting CBO campaign
cards.summary: Group each batch of new creatives into its own ad set in a CBO prospecting campaign so new concepts compete with each other on the same budget.
cards.use_when: You are setting up campaign structure to test a new batch of creative concepts and deciding how to organize ad sets.

cards.title: Force early spend on new ads with a 1x-CPA ad set minimum
cards.summary: Set an ad set minimum daily spend equal to 1x your target CPA for 7 days to prevent new creatives from starving behind older winning ads.
cards.use_when: New ad sets are getting almost no delivery because older ads hog the budget, and you need to test them quickly.

cards.title: Analyze winners with incremental attribution and a spend/ROAS threshold
cards.summary: Review ad performance using incremental attribution, sort by spend, and flag high-spend ads that beat your brand's ROAS threshold as iteration candidates.
cards.use_when: You are running the analysis step of a creative testing cycle and deciding which ads to iterate or scale.

cards.title: Iterate off your own winners to complete the creative flywheel
cards.summary: Duplicate, vary, and merge your best-performing ads the same way you do competitors, feeding results back into continuous testing.
cards.use_when: You have identified high-spend, above-threshold winning ads and want to extend their life and solidify core concepts.

cards.title: Judge ads by total profit across concepts, not a single top ROAS
cards.summary: Run a portfolio of concepts where profitable high-spend and lower-spend winners coexist, rather than chasing only the highest ROAS ad.
cards.use_when: You are deciding which ad concepts to keep, scale, or cut based on ROAS versus spend capacity.

cards.title: Build a predictable creative machine instead of duplicating old ads
cards.summary: Replace ad-hoc creative production (duplicate winners or mass-produce UGC) with a repeatable system that raises the win rate of new concepts.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to keep pumping out volume-based creative or invest in a structured creative production and testing workflow.

cards.title: The 33% Rule for Creative Sourcing
cards.summary: Split ad creative production roughly into thirds across in-house, UGC creator army, and AI so volume, authenticity and control are all covered.
cards.use_when: Planning monthly creative production volume for a Meta ad account and deciding where the next batch of ads should come from.

cards.title: Creator Army Sourcing Workflow (Sample Seeding to Ad Account)
cards.summary: Send mass creator invites, ship product samples, and require 2-3 videos per sample so you build an always-on pool of UGC for TikTok and Meta.
cards.use_when: Building or replenishing UGC ad supply for Meta and TikTok, or resetting creative volume after a launch or offer change.

cards.title: Brief Creators Wide vs Specific to Steer Winning Formats
cards.summary: Use open-ended briefs to surface new angles and specific briefs pointing at proven top ads to multiply winners you already know.
cards.use_when: Onboarding a creator army or a new batch of UGC creators and deciding what instructions to give them.

cards.title: Map Ad Creatives to Buyer Awareness Stages
cards.summary: Break creatives into unaware, problem, solution, product and most-aware formats so Meta's algorithm can serve the right message at the right moment.
cards.use_when: Building a new ad set or auditing an existing one to see whether the creative mix covers the full buyer journey.

cards.title: Test a broader creative portfolio when one format dominates spend
cards.summary: The source recommends distinct formats and angles to reduce dependence on a few winners; validate with store economics.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to iterate on a single winning ad or invest in new formats, or diagnosing sudden ROAS decay after scaling.

cards.title: Diagnosing Creative Fatigue Across the Lifetime of a Winning Ad
cards.summary: Map how ROAS responds to rising spend — variant-only campaigns decay in cycles; distinct-format portfolios hold longer.
cards.use_when: Interpreting an account whose ROAS declined after a spend increase, or forecasting whether a current creative set can absorb planned scale.
